questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state why abrasive working is required in hard stone
questions.stem: A sculptor is asked to finish a block of grey granite with a smooth, rounded surface. Which method is physically capable of that result, and why is that method used?

options.text: Grinding and polishing with mineral grit, because the rock is harder than any metal edge can bite into
Chiselling it away with hardened steel, because steel is the hardest tool a working shop can own
options.misconception: assumes a steel chisel can cut granite, when metal tools cannot work the rock at all

options.text: Casting it in a two-piece mould, because a stone of that hardness cannot be shaped by hand at all
options.misconception: treats carved stone as a cast object, borrowing bronze and clay workshop practice

options.text: Splitting it with wooden wedges driven along the bedding, because granite splits like a layered rock
options.misconception: believes granite cleaves cleanly along planes, a property of slate and schist

questions.explanation: Granite is one of the hardest stones a workshop meets: its interlocking crystals are harder than any tool made of metal, so an edge cannot be pressed into it. Cutting is done instead by abrasion, driving a harder mineral grit across the surface with a stone or metal tool, and the grit is what removes the material. The consequence runs through the whole tradition: undercut and pierced work is impractical, fine detail is expensive, and a polished surface is the normal finish, because smoothness is what abrasion can actually deliver. The tempting belief is that hardness is decided by the tool. In stone the tool never wins.
questions.hint: Ask what a metal edge can actually do to this rock, and what removes the material instead.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what direct carving commits a carver to
questions.stem: A carver in stone is described as cutting directly, with no model, no armature and no full-size drawing on the block. What does that description say about how the figure arrives?

options.text: It is subtracted from the block itself, so every decision becomes final as the stone comes away
It is assembled afterwards from separately carved limbs fitted into a prepared core
options.misconception: believes a stone figure is built up from joined parts, as a bronze can be

options.text: It is traced from a full-size cartoon laid over the face of the uncut stone before cutting
options.misconception: believes direct carving still depends on a full-size transferred drawing

options.text: It is modelled first in wax, which is burnt out and replaced by stone poured into the space
options.misconception: borrows the lost-wax casting sequence and applies it to a stone carving

questions.explanation: Direct carving is subtractive: the figure exists only as what is left when the unwanted stone has gone, and the block dictates the answer. The carver is committed at the first cut, because stone removed cannot be replaced and a part taken too far cannot be returned. That commitment is why the block's own character shows in the result, since bedding planes, veins and inclusions are discovered as the work proceeds and often decide the design. A cast object hides the process completely, because the material is poured into a prepared space rather than cut away.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to stone once it has been removed, and whether it can be put back.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what follows from a sculpture being carved in place
questions.stem: The great lion-bodied monument at Giza was cut down into a natural knoll of rock left standing in the desert floor, and the surrounding enclosure walls serve as its flanks. What follows from those facts?

options.text: The figure was never quarried or moved, and the carver cut into the floor around the natural mass
The figure was quarried in sections and reassembled, since no single block was large enough
options.misconception: believes the monument was assembled from transported blocks, as built architecture is

options.text: The head and the body were taken from two separate outcrops and joined together at the neck
options.misconception: believes the two ends of the figure came from separate sources and were later joined

options.text: The figure was cast from a model excavated in the rock and then set against the wall
options.misconception: treats a carved stone monument as a cast object, importing bronze workshop practice

questions.explanation: Because the rock was never detached, the work has no quarry stage, no transport stage and no setting stage. The enclosure walls are not architecture added later; they are the negative space left when the surrounding floor was cut away, and the body's tapering sides are carved, not built. The original bedding of the rock can still be traced around the flanks, which is exactly what one expects of a figure cut from a single mass in place. The belief that great stone figures are assembled from blocks belongs to building work, not to this kind of carving.
questions.hint: Ask whether a rock that was never lifted from the ground can show quarry seams or transport marks.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a lost-wax mould cannot be reused
questions.stem: In lost-wax casting a wax model is enclosed in a mould, and the wax is melted or burnt out before molten metal is poured into the space. Why is that mould then finished for good?

options.text: The wax has to be destroyed to open the space the metal fills, so the mould is broken to free it
Bronze contracts as it cools, so a mould must never be allowed to touch the casting again
options.misconception: invents a shrinkage rule for moulds that does not explain why they are broken

options.text: Clay cannot survive the heat of molten metal, so every mould cracks on the first pour
options.misconception: blames the heat of the pour, when the mould is designed to be broken anyway

options.text: The wax model can be reused, so a second pour would produce an identical second casting
options.misconception: believes the wax survives, which is the one thing the process removes

questions.explanation: The whole point of the lost-wax method is that the wax is sacrificed: it is the temporary filling that makes a one-off mould possible, so a complex undercuts, which a rigid two-piece mould could not release, can be modelled in wax and then cast. Once the metal has cooled, the mould has to be broken and taken off the bronze, so it is spent. That is also why a unique bronze cannot simply be repeated; a copy requires a new mould taken from the finished object. Treating the mould as durable equipment mistakes the method for a reusable foundry form.
questions.hint: Ask what has to disappear from the mould before any metal can occupy that space.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: describe the surface an old bronze develops
questions.stem: A bronze that stood outdoors for centuries is covered by a dull green surface that has become part of the object. What is that layer?

options.text: A patina of corrosion products, which forms as the alloy weathers and slows further change
A coloured wax laid on by the founder so the bronze would read as weathered from the start
options.misconception: assumes the green was deliberately applied when the statue was new

options.text: The red priming coat of the foundry, showing through where the bronze never reached
options.misconception: reads a buried foundry coat as if it were the finished surface

options.text: An old layer of varnish, applied indoors and now darkened by exposure to daylight
options.misconception: believes a protective coating can turn green by itself over centuries

questions.explanation: Bronze is a copper alloy, and the green surface is the family of copper corrosion products that form where air, moisture and salts have acted on the metal. The patina is at once a record of the object's history and a protective layer, because the dense outer products slow further attack. A dark brown surface on outdoor sculpture is a different case: that is very often an applied wax or oil, aged and handled, and the two look similar but are not the same thing. The general point is that the surface of an old bronze is mostly history, not original finish.
questions.hint: Ask what bronze is made of, and what those metals do when air, water and salts reach them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: apply the movement of wood to the choice of panel thickness
questions.stem: Wood swells and shrinks as the air around it changes, and it moves far more across the grain than along it. How does that fact constrain the board used for a panel painting?

options.text: The board must be thin enough to move as one piece, or its coating splits where the wood bends
The board must be as thick as possible, because a thick block simply does not change shape
options.misconception: believes thickness cancels wood movement instead of magnifying it

options.text: The board must be cut so the grain runs in two directions at once, which cancels movement
options.misconception: imagines a cross-grain construction that could balance out hygroscopic movement

options.text: The board must be nailed at the edges to a frame, so the frame holds the wood still
options.misconception: believes a rigid frame prevents the board itself from swelling

questions.explanation: Wood is hygroscopic and moves most across the grain, so a thick block changes shape unevenly: its face and its edges, and its two ends, respond differently, and the block cups and twists. A thin board, especially a well-seasoned one, moves much more like a single flexible piece, so the ground and paint film on it bend together. This is why panels were made from boards of limited width, often joined, and why wide later panels crack across their grain. The trap is to treat thickness as strength; here thickness is the problem.
questions.hint: Ask what a thick block does to its own faces and edges as the humidity rises and falls.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The chalk ground on a panel
questions.learningObjective: state what a chalk and glue ground provides
questions.stem: A carver's wooden panel is covered coat after coat with chalk and animal glue until the surface is smooth, level and white. What does that layer give the painter to work on?

options.text: A smooth, light ground on which a hairline drawing and thin paint sit cleanly
A surface that stretches with the wood, so the paint cannot crack as the panel moves
options.misconception: believes a rigid chalk ground can stretch with the support beneath it

options.text: A darker field than bare wood, which makes the bright colours and gold read brighter
options.misconception: claims a white ground darkens the panel instead of lightening it

options.text: A fixative that binds the colours permanently, so they can never be lifted or repainted
options.misconception: treats a preparatory ground as though it fixed the finished picture

questions.explanation: The ground of chalk and glue, laid in several thin coats and levelled smooth, gives a surface that is flat, white and even. Flatness is what lets a fine drawn line and a thin stroke of paint read at all on a rough plank, and whiteness matters technically: light ground reflects incoming light back up through thin translucent layers, which is part of the luminous effect in old panel painting. It is rigid, not elastic, and it is a preparation for painting rather than part of the picture, so it fixes nothing and it darkens nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what a painter could not do on a rough, absorbent board, and how light colours depend on a white base.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: explain why the weave of a linen canvas can stay visible
questions.stem: On an oil painting on linen, the pattern of the threads is still readable in the thinnest passages of the sky. What accounts for that?

options.text: The weave is a physical ridge and valley, and a film thinner than that relief cannot cover it
The threads repel the oily binder, so the paint sits only on the raised crossings of the weave
options.misconception: believes linen repels oil, when the oil is held by a sizing on the fibres

options.text: The glue size was spread unevenly, so the thread tops take colour and the hollows do not
options.misconception: blames uneven sizing for a pattern that is simply the fabric's structure

options.text: The linen was woven far too coarsely, so no painter could have covered the threads at all
options.misconception: judges the weave by the flattest passages and ignores the whole surface

questions.explanation: Canvas is not a flat surface but a topography of crossed threads, and paint thinner than that relief simply follows it instead of hiding it. This is why thin glazes and scumbles let the weave show while an impasto passage buries it, and why painters who wanted a smooth surface chose a finer, tighter weave. The visible weave is also evidence: a fine, regular, machine-like weave points to a later date, and the thickness of the cloth is recorded in inventories for exactly that reason. Nothing in the picture is failing; the support is simply still there.
questions.hint: Ask how thick a film of paint is compared with the height of the threads themselves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose of sizing
questions.stem: A linen canvas is soaked in a thin glue solution before any ground or paint goes onto it. What is that step, called sizing, actually for?

options.text: To fill the absorbent fibres, so they cannot drink the oil binder out of the paint applied later
To make the finished support completely rigid, so the painting can never flex again
options.misconception: believes sizing aims at total rigidity rather than at controlling absorbency

options.text: To bleach the linen to an even white, so its natural colour does not show through the paint
options.misconception: confuses the purpose of sizing with the whitening that the lead ground achieves

options.text: To tighten the weave, so the threads become finer and the paint sits on them more smoothly
options.misconception: believes sizing physically closes the weave of the cloth

questions.explanation: Raw linen is wicking, so oil applied to it is drawn deep into the fibres and away from the surface. The result is paint that sinks in, dries dull, binds badly and darkens, and a picture that looks quite different once a ground is added. Sizing, a dilute animal or oil glue, partly fills the porous fibres and reduces that suction, so the film stays on the surface where the painter can see and control it. Sizing is a control on absorption, not a stiffening coat and not a bleach.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to an oil film laid on raw, thirsty linen.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state how an egg binder changes the working method
questions.stem: Egg tempera is pigment mixed with egg yolk and thinned with water. What does that binder do to the painter's working method?

options.text: It sets within minutes, so form must be built from small strokes instead of blended wet
It sets by taking up air over hours, so strokes can be blended and softened at leisure
options.misconception: gives tempera the slow oxidation that belongs to an oil binder

options.text: It stays wet for days in a closed room, so a passage can be reworked freely
options.misconception: believes the binder resists drying altogether in an enclosed space

options.text: It cures into a film that can be scraped and repainted without disturbing what lies under it
options.misconception: believes a dried tempera film can be cut back like a cured varnish

questions.explanation: Tempera dries by losing water to the air, and it does so in minutes rather than hours. That single fact reorganises the whole method: there is no open time in which to blend, so form is built from many small hatched strokes laid side by side, and a passage cannot be returned to once it is dry, because a fresh wet stroke lifts the earlier one instead of merging with it. A painter's written instructions from the period stress exactly this. Oil binders reverse every one of those limits, which is why the two media produce surfaces that look and behave so differently.
questions.hint: Ask what has to leave the paint for it to set, and how quickly that happens in a warm room.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why an oil binder gives longer working time
questions.stem: A painter finds that an oil passage can be blended, softened and re-opened for hours, while a tempera passage cannot be touched at all once it has begun to set. What accounts for that difference?

options.text: Linseed oil hardens by taking up oxygen from the air, a slow reaction, not by losing water quickly
Linseed oil loses its water very slowly, so its drying rate depends on droplet size
options.misconception: describes evaporation, which is the mechanism of tempera, and not of oil

options.text: Linseed oil does not dry at all, and it is made to set by a drier added at the end
options.misconception: believes oil is non-drying and that drying is added as a final ingredient

options.text: Linseed oil dries at once, and the extra working time comes from warming the studio
options.misconception: invents a studio temperature rule to explain what is a chemical change

questions.explanation: Drying oil does not dry by evaporating a solvent, because there is no solvent to evaporate; the liquid itself is the binder. It hardens because the unsaturated fatty acids it contains react with oxygen from the air, a slow oxidation that can be catalysed by the lead driers painters add. That slowness is a gift: it buys blending, wet-into-wet work, thick impasto, and time to lay one translucent glaze over another. The cost is that the surface skins over, that dust settles into it, and that a picture may not be safe to varnish for months.
questions.hint: Ask what linseed oil takes from the air, and what tempera loses.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the function of the monochrome underpainting
questions.stem: In a well-made tempera panel the artist first lays in a monochrome layer of greenish or grey colour, then builds the finished colours over it. What has that first layer already settled?

options.text: The light, the shade and the whole drawing, so the colour layers land on a decided value plan
The dampness of the panel, so the colour above it cannot be lifted off the surface
options.misconception: believes a monochrome underpainting is there to seal the panel against damp

options.text: The underdrawing, in a fine dark line that the colour layers then follow exactly
options.misconception: mistakes a tonal underpainting for the drawn design that precedes it

options.text: The errors in the design, covering them so the finished image needs no correction at all
options.misconception: supposes the underpainting exists to bury mistakes rather than to plan values

questions.explanation: Because tempera cannot be blended, the painter has to know the light and shade before colour enters the picture. A monochrome layer in grey or in a greenish grey, often called verdaccio, fixes the tonal structure and the drawing; colour is then applied over it in thin strokes, and the pale ground and the light underpainting show through to give the characteristic luminosity. The drawn design, in a brush line, metalpoint or ink, is a separate and earlier stage. Getting the two confused is easy because both lie under the colour.
questions.hint: Ask what a grey-green layer can decide before any hue is committed to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: correct the claim that oil painting was invented in one moment
questions.stem: It is often said that a famous fifteenth-century northern painter invented oil painting. What does the record from earlier centuries show instead?

options.text: Pigments ground in drying oils were documented in use across Europe and Asia long before his career
Nothing at all, since the technique was unknown anywhere and rests on that one claim alone
options.misconception: accepts a single late account as the whole of the evidence

options.text: That he found an old recipe in a manuscript and was the first to put it into practice
options.misconception: credits him with recovering a lost written recipe rather than with technique

options.text: That oils were known but unusable, until somebody found the right way to grind the pigment
options.misconception: believes binders and pigments were incompatible until a discovery joined them

questions.explanation: Oil-bound paints appear in the record for centuries before the fifteenth century, in panel painting, in manuscript illumination and in craft recipes across Europe and the Islamic world. The story that one northern painter invented the medium is a later construction, repeated from an early biographer's remark and amplified in the nineteenth century, and it survives because it makes a clean origin story out of a gradual development. What is genuinely creditable to him is the exploitation of a slow-drying binder in thin translucent layers, which is a way of using oil rather than the invention of oil.
questions.hint: Ask what the record shows about oil-bound paints a century or two earlier.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the physical fact that governs fresco
questions.stem: A wall painter is working in buon fresco, applying pigment to a freshly laid coat of lime plaster. What physical fact governs the whole method?

options.text: The plaster takes the colour as it hardens, so the picture becomes part of the wall itself
The plaster must already be dry and sealed, so nothing can change once the coats have set
options.misconception: describes the dry-wall method that fresco exists to avoid

options.text: The colour has to be fired in a kiln, so the wall must be baked with the picture still wet
options.misconception: imports the firing step of ceramic painting into a wall

options.text: The pigment has to be mixed with wax, so the wall is polished flat between every layer
options.misconception: confuses a wall painting with a wax-enamel technique

questions.explanation: Lime plaster is a suspension that dries by taking up carbon dioxide from the air, and as it becomes carbonate it forms a crystalline network that locks whatever is in it. Pigment brushed into the water of the wet coat is therefore caught inside the wall, which is why the surface of a fresco is matte and why the picture cannot be cleaned with solvent without taking plaster with it. The picture and its support are one object: a section of a fresco wall is a piece of wall, not a removable skin. That is the whole constraint the technique accepts.
questions.hint: Ask what lime does as it dries, and where the pigment has to be when that happens.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish fresco secco from buon fresco
questions.stem: In a cold cell, a painter ground pigment in a binding medium and laid it onto plaster that had dried weeks earlier. What is that method called, and what follows from it for the picture?

options.text: Fresco secco, and the colour sits in a film on the surface that can flake away with it
Buon fresco, and the colour has locked into the plaster and can never be removed
options.misconception: calls a dry-wall painting buon fresco and credits it with impossible adhesion

options.text: Tempera on a panel, so the wall counts as an ordinary flat support like a board
options.misconception: treats a wall as though it behaved like a portable wooden support

options.text: Encaustic, so the wall must first have been heated to melt the wax into the surface
options.misconception: insists on a heat step that the described method does not involve

questions.explanation: When the colour is applied to dry plaster with a binder, adhesion depends entirely on that added film, because the wall can no longer lock anything in. The consequence is mechanical rather than chemical: the layer can flake, powder or be lost with the plaster beneath it, and it does so unpredictably over centuries. The reward is freedom. Work on a dry surface can be done slowly, revised, and finished with detail that would be impossible in a day's patch of wet plaster, which is why it was standard in colder climates and for finishing touches on a fresco wall.
questions.hint: Ask what holds the colour on: the wall itself, or a film the painter added?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Day-sized sections of a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fresco wall is worked in day-sized sections
questions.stem: A fresco painter lays the fine plaster and paints a patch within a single working day, then starts a new patch the next morning. What problem does that division of the wall solve?

options.text: Only wet plaster will take the colour, so a day's patch must be finished before it dries
Ground pigment keeps for a day once mixed with water, so nothing may be kept overnight
options.misconception: believes the pigment spoils, when it is the plaster that has to be used wet

options.text: Only one apprentice could be paid to handle wet plaster at a time in a small workshop
options.misconception: reduces a technical necessity to an economic one

options.text: The patron inspected and approved every section before the next one was begun
options.misconception: supplies a documentary routine that is not the reason for the sections

questions.explanation: The unit of work is the day because the day is the working life of a patch of fine plaster. A large area plastered at once would dry unevenly, and the painter would be stopped by a dry patch in the middle of a figure, unable to return to it. Working in day-sized sections keeps each patch inside its own workable time; the joins between patches are the seams still visible in many frescoes, and painters plan compositions around them. Each day's material is also prepared the evening before, so the morning goes entirely on painting.
questions.hint: Ask how long a laid coat of fine plaster stays workable, and what a painter does at the end of that time.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A wall painting on a dry support
questions.learningObjective: apply the plaster constraint to explain a damaged wall painting
questions.stem: The Last Supper in the Milanese refectory began flaking soon after it was finished, and much of its lower part has since been lost. Why did it decay far faster than a fresco wall would have?

options.text: It was painted with binder onto a dry wall, so the film was only ever resting on the surface
It was painted into wet plaster, but too little lime was used and the wall never set properly
options.misconception: invents a faulty plaster mix to explain damage that the technique explains

options.text: It was painted on a dry wall because dry plaster gives a brighter and more lasting colour
options.misconception: accepts a dry-wall technique and credits it with the very durability it lacks

options.text: It was varnished when new, and the varnish hardened and cracked together with the wall
options.misconception: blames an added protective film that the described technique does not use

questions.explanation: The painter wanted the control and the range of colour that a slow-drying medium on a dry surface gives, and accepted the cost knowingly: nothing locked into the masonry, so the layer was only ever attached to it. Damp rising in a refectory, together with a film that could not bond, allowed the paint to lift. Successive campaigns of repair and cleaning, including retouching on dry plaster in later centuries, each altered the surface further, so the surviving picture is the result of a long series of decisions, not one accident.
questions.hint: Ask whether the picture ever became part of the wall, and what the moisture in a refectory would then do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what thick paint contributes to a picture
questions.stem: In several passages the paint has been laid on so thickly that the ridges of the brush and the scrape of a palette knife stand out in raking light. What has the painter gained by this?

options.text: Real relief in the surface, so the light on the ridges changes as the viewer moves
A sharper image, since a thick film carries more detail and blurs less than a thin one
options.misconception: believes thickness produces optical sharpness, which depends on drawing instead

options.text: A larger picture, since thick paint spreads outward as it is pushed across the support
options.misconception: treats paint as though it expanded to enlarge the work

options.text: A sealed surface, since a thick film fixes the colours beneath it permanently
options.misconception: believes the thickest passages varnish the picture and lock it

questions.explanation: Paint applied thickly behaves as material rather than as colour: ridges catch light and throw small shadows, so the picture has an illumination of its own that shifts as the viewer moves. Texture also carries information a drawn image cannot, since a raised stroke can describe a lit edge, a dragging movement or a modelled form in one act. Many painters thinned and mixed colours on the surface with a knife. The costs are real as well: thick paint ages differently from thin, can cup or crack, and can be cut by careless cleaning.
questions.hint: Ask what light does to a surface that is not actually flat.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the depth cue supplied by one-point perspective
questions.stem: A painter constructs a tiled floor in one-point linear perspective, drawing every row of joints so that it runs back toward one point. Which device is doing the work that makes the far end read as far away?

options.text: The receding parallel edges are drawn as lines that converge on a single vanishing point
The far part of the floor is painted paler and cooler than the near part, in lower contrast
options.misconception: mistakes the atmospheric cue for the linear one and the reverse as well

options.text: The tiles at the far end are drawn smaller than near tiles that are exactly the same size
options.misconception: credits diminution, a separate cue, for what the construction itself contributes

options.text: The near tiles are outlined heavily, so they separate crisply from the floor behind them
options.misconception: credits a heavy contour, which is a device of clarity rather than of depth

questions.explanation: The device named by the method is convergence: parallel edges that recede from the eye are drawn as lines meeting at a point, and because they meet, the eye reads them as going away. A correct construction also makes the far tiles smaller and does the same to their contrast, so several cues work together, but they are separate devices with separate names. Mixing them up is easy and harmless in a picture, and it matters in a test: the linear cue is the only one that needs a vanishing point, and only it is available without touching colour.
questions.hint: Ask which element of the construction is not a matter of colour or outline at all.

questions.learningObjective: identify the cue that atmospheric perspective relies on
questions.stem: A landscape grows paler, cooler and lower in contrast as it recedes, while a tree at the front edge is drawn with a hard dark contour. What is producing the sense of distance in that picture?

options.text: Atmospheric perspective, working by lost contrast and a cooling of colour with distance
Linear perspective, working by converging parallel edges on a vanishing point
options.misconception: names the linear cue where the colour cue is doing the work

options.text: Foreshortening, working by compressing a form as it turns away from the eye
options.misconception: names the compression of forms, which is not a distance cue at all

options.text: Hierarchical scale, working by enlarging whatever matters most in the scene
options.misconception: confuses a rule about importance with a rule about distance

questions.explanation: Light travelling through air is scattered, so the farther an object stands the more the atmosphere mixes into it: contrast falls, edges soften, and colour shifts away from warm towards cool and pale. That is a cue the eye uses about distance without any geometry at all, which is why it survives in painting long after the other cues were formalised and why landscapes rely on it heavily. The confusion to avoid is with scale: making a figure larger in a picture says who matters, not how far away it stands, and those two rules can and do contradict each other.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: locate the vanishing point in a one-point construction
questions.stem: In a one-point perspective construction of a room, where does the vanishing point for the orthogonals of the floor and side walls sit in relation to the picture?

options.text: On the horizon line, at a distance from the picture plane set by the chosen viewing position
At the centre of the panel, where the diagonal of the rectangle happens to cross
options.misconception: puts the point at the centre of the support instead of on the horizon

options.text: On the ground line at the foot of the nearest column, which fixes the size of the room
options.misconception: confuses the base of the nearest object with a point of convergence

options.text: Behind the picture surface at infinity, since parallel lines never really meet anywhere
options.misconception: treats a mathematical limit as a point the picture contains

questions.explanation: Every orthogonal in a one-point construction is parallel to the floor and to one another, and all of them converge on a single point. That point lies on the horizon line, because orthogonals run at the same level as the eye and can only meet at their own height. Where it sits along the horizon, and therefore how far behind the wall it appears to be, is fixed by where the artist has placed the viewer, which is a decision rather than a measurement. Two more vanishing points appear as soon as the sets of parallel edges are not parallel to the picture plane.
questions.hint: Ask which single straight line in the picture must contain the point where receding parallels meet.

questions.topic: Horizon at the level of the eye
questions.learningObjective: infer the implied viewer from the position of the horizon
questions.stem: In a constructed interior the horizon line sits exactly at eye level for an adult standing on the floor shown. What does that choice tell a viewer about the picture?

options.text: It fixes the implied viewer as a standing adult of that height, standing inside the room
It records the painter's own height, since a horizon is a direct measurement of the artist
options.misconception: treats the horizon as biographical evidence about the painter's body

options.text: It proves the room is taller than its furniture, so the furnishings must be out of scale
options.misconception: turns a claim about the viewer into a claim about the accuracy of the room

options.text: It requires the picture to be hung above eye level, so the horizon is above the visitor
options.misconception: inverts the advice normally given about hanging a constructed interior

questions.explanation: The horizon in a mathematically constructed picture is the level of the viewer's own eye, so putting it at the eye level of a standing adult is a claim about who is supposed to be looking. The room is then built around a body of that height at that position, and the viewer reads the picture as a place one could occupy. The related practical point is that such a picture is normally hung with its horizon at the eye level of a visitor, since the composition is composed for a particular relation between picture and body. Paintings do record how artists saw, but a horizon is a decision first.
questions.hint: Ask what height the horizon in a constructed interior stands for.

questions.learningObjective: identify foreshortening and the cue it produces
questions.stem: A reclining figure holds one foot out towards the viewer with the sole turned towards the picture. Which device describes what the painter has done to that foot?

options.text: Projected it along the line of sight, so its length is compressed and it overlaps the shin
Drawn it beside the shin, so that both keep their full length side by side on the surface
options.misconception: suggests the two forms are laid out in profile with no shortening at all

options.text: Enlarged it beyond the shin, so the eye is pulled to it as the nearest object
options.misconception: uses size instead of compression to make a form come forward

options.text: Placed it on the horizon line, so that it can be seen whole from directly beside
options.misconception: suggests that position on the horizon is what reveals a form completely

questions.explanation: A form pointing towards the viewer is turned away from the picture plane, and the part of it that points at the eye is the part that lies edge-on. Drawing it means projecting it along the line of sight, so its apparent length collapses while its cross-section stays legible, and it necessarily overlaps what is behind it. That overlap, plus the loss of length, is the cue. Foreshortening is what makes a body seen from below or from above readable, and it is the reason painted ceilings can look like real space.
questions.hint: Ask how a form pointing at the eye appears when its length is laid flat on the surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify depth cues that need no geometry
questions.stem: A painter draws a road into the distance with no converging lines at all, using only three devices: near things are placed low in the picture, far things are placed high, and nearer forms cover parts of farther ones. What is at work?

options.text: Placement and overlap within the picture plane, which are depth cues needing no vanishing point
Atmospheric perspective, which depends on pale colour and reduced contrast with distance
options.misconception: credits a colour cue that the description explicitly leaves out

options.text: Foreshortening, which compresses every form as it turns away from the eye
options.misconception: names a cue for forms turned in depth, not for a road seen from above

options.text: One-point perspective, which requires a horizon set at the viewer's own eye level
options.misconception: claims a geometric construction the description rules out

questions.explanation: Objects higher in the picture are read as further away, and an object drawn over another is read as nearer, because in ordinary vision those two regularities hold almost every time. That is enough to build depth in a landscape or a battle scene without a single vanishing point, and it is how depth was handled for centuries before perspective was formalised. The set of such regularities is the standard list of pictorial depth cues, and perspective is only one member of it, though it is the one that turned the list into a system.
questions.hint: Ask whether the picture uses any geometry at all, or only the arrangement of shapes on its surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Size as a statement of rank
questions.learningObjective: interpret a difference in figure size
questions.stem: On a carved relief a standing ruler is cut noticeably larger than the officials beside him, and all the figures stand on the same ground line. What is the difference in size doing?

options.text: Asserting higher rank, since relative size is read as importance rather than as distance
Showing the ruler stands closer to the viewer than the officials do
options.misconception: reads a rank statement as a claim about optical distance

options.text: Correcting a carver's error, since one figure was never finished or measured
options.misconception: assumes the difference is a mistake rather than a decision

options.text: Compensating for the ruler standing on a higher step cut into the ground line
options.misconception: invents a step that the description says is not there

questions.explanation: When a picture does not offer convincing evidence about how far away each figure stands, the eye falls back on what it takes size to mean, and in a formal court or ritual context that is rank. A ruler carved larger than his attendants, all on one line and at the same ground level, is making a claim about order rather than about optics, and the claim is the point of the relief. The trap is to read every difference of size as depth. Where a picture does establish distance convincingly, size measures distance; where it does not, it measures importance.
questions.hint: Ask what size usually means in a picture, and whether a shared ground line rules out distance.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a register arrangement establishes
questions.stem: The figures on an ancient painted wall are arranged in horizontal bands of even height, evenly spaced, each running the full width and each separated by a ruled line. What does that arrangement set up?

options.text: Ranked tiers, in which a figure's height above the baseline states its standing in the order
A single shared ground line, so that all the figures stand equally far from the viewer
options.misconception: misreads a set of bands as one continuous floor space

options.text: A continuous landscape, in which the bands mark the near, middle and far distance
options.misconception: turns a symbolic layering into a measured recession of space

options.text: A single instant, in which the bands are stacking the figures on top of one another
options.misconception: confuses the order of the tiers with the order of events

questions.explanation: Bands give the picture an explicit order without proposing a place. Each band has its own baseline, so the size of a figure and the tier it occupies can be read as statements of rank, and the ruled lines keep the reading separate from any suggestion of one continuous space. The same arrangement also lets a sequence be read in a fixed order, whether that is a list of conquered places or a series of scenes arranged around the viewer. Later painters broke this up precisely in order to construct a single room in which the tiers no longer mean what they used to.
questions.hint: Ask what a ruled horizontal band does that a single floor space cannot do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Profile head with a frontal eye
questions.learningObjective: explain the convention of a profile head and frontal eye
questions.stem: In a figure drawn in the ancient Egyptian manner the head is turned to the side so the nose and chin are in profile, yet the eye is drawn as though seen from the front. Why is the head treated in two ways at once?

options.text: Each part is shown from the angle in which it is most recognisable, since clarity outranks optical truth
The figure is turning its head, and the painter recorded the two halves of the movement
options.misconception: reads a convention as a description of a physical motion

options.text: The eye must be frontal because painters had not yet worked out how to draw one in profile
options.misconception: invents a technical inability that the same pictures disprove

options.text: The head is a portrait of one person and the body belongs to another, set side by side
options.misconception: turns a single figure into two unrelated sitters

questions.explanation: A profile shows the shape of a head and the line of a nose; a frontal eye shows the pupil, the lid and the brow, which in profile would be reduced to an edge. The convention takes the most legible presentation of each part and assembles them into a figure that is clear, stable and readable from the side, which is where a figure in a procession or a band is actually seen. The same logic runs through the rest of the body, where the shoulders and the eye of a profile figure are both shown frontally. The claim that the convention is a failure of technique is contradicted by the profile eye, which is drawn in profile elsewhere in the same tradition.
questions.hint: Ask what each of those two views makes legible, and whether they could both be true at once.

questions.topic: The effect of a gold ground
questions.learningObjective: state what a gold ground does to depicted space
questions.stem: A carved and painted panel sets its figures against a flat field of gold leaf with no floor, no sky and no landscape. What has the gold done to the space the figures appear in?

options.text: It supplies no depth cues at all, so the figures read against an undefined luminous field
It creates depth by mirroring the figures faintly in the gold behind them
options.misconception: believes the leaf acts as a mirror image of the scene

options.text: It creates depth by catching the light of an unseen window across the room's walls
options.misconception: invents a room behind the field, when the gold stands for no such room

options.text: It places the scene outdoors, since gold always stands for the sky in a painted panel
options.misconception: reads the gold as a specific location rather than as an absence of one

questions.explanation: Gold leaf is achromatic and non-representational: it names no place, no hour and no light source, and it gives no recession, no scale and no ground for a figure to stand on. A figure against it therefore floats in front of a luminous field rather than standing somewhere, which is exactly what made the gold useful in churches, where the subject was not a place at all. Painters who wanted space kept the gold for figures and the frame and introduced a sky and a landscape behind them, which produces the uneasy mixture of two different kinds of space in one picture.
questions.hint: Ask what cues of distance a flat metal surface can supply, and how far gold can read as a place.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose of burnishing gilding
questions.stem: Gold leaf is laid over a layer of red clay, wetted so the leaf will hold, and then rubbed with an agate tool until the surface shines. What is the burnishing step for?

options.text: Compacting the leaf into a continuous film, so it reflects as metal instead of as separate squares
Thinning the leaf, so the red clay shows through and warms the gold
options.misconception: believes burnishing removes gold and reveals the preparation beneath

options.text: Pressing the leaf into the grain, so it can never be lifted from the panel again
options.misconception: confuses burnishing with a fixing method, though burnishing is a surface action

options.text: Removing the gold entirely, leaving a polished red ground to be painted over
options.misconception: makes burnishing a stripping process, which is a conservation decision

questions.explanation: Leaf laid loosely catches light at many different angles at once and reads as a scatter of dull flecks. Burnishing flattens the leaf, closes the joins between squares and compacts it onto the bole beneath, so the surface begins to reflect as one continuous skin of metal, and the red clay underneath is warmed by that reflection. The gilder can also add small patterns of burnished and unburnished gold to make the surface carry light differently across a garment. Nothing about the step removes material, which is why it is a finishing operation.
questions.hint: Ask what changes physically when loose squares of leaf are worked into a surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: compare a painted surface with a display screen
questions.stem: A picture on a canvas exists as material: pigment, binder and support, physically present whether or not anyone is looking. An image on a display screen behaves differently. What is the essential difference?

options.text: The screen's image is a pattern of light from an array of elements, and it exists only while powered
The screen's image is stored in the glass, so it survives exactly as long as a painting does
options.misconception: believes a display holds a durable image in its own material, like a print

options.text: The screen's image is painted with light-sensitive pigment, so it behaves like a print
options.misconception: mistakes a light-emitting surface for a light-sensitive one

options.text: The screen's image is a single continuous surface, while a canvas is made of separate threads
options.misconception: compares the physical composition of the two supports, not their behaviour

questions.explanation: A display makes its picture by emitting light from a grid of elements, each with its own colour and brightness, so the image is a light field in front of the surface and not a deposit on it. It depends on a power source, on a viewing environment and on the refresh of the elements, which is why screens need adjusting, mirror badly and look different in daylight. A painted or printed picture is a stable object that can be carried into any light. The medium of the screen is therefore the lighting of the room, which is a real constraint on how such images are made and judged.
questions.hint: Ask what a screen actually puts out into the room, and what happens to that when the power is cut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: describe what a camera obscura does to an image
questions.stem: A draughtsman darkens a small room, fits a convex lens into a hole in the shutter so daylight can enter, and works on a sheet of paper fixed to the opposite wall. Which statement about that arrangement is right?

options.text: The lens forms an inverted real image of the view outside, and the artist traces the projected lines
The lens throws an upright image on the paper, so the artist can copy it without reversing anything
options.misconception: believes the projected image is upright, when a single lens reverses it

options.text: The lens simply brightens the room, so that the paper can be seen without darkening the shutters
options.misconception: treats the device as a lamp rather than as an image-forming instrument

options.text: The lens records the view permanently on its own glass, so nothing has to be drawn afterwards
options.misconception: believes the image is captured on the lens instead of being projected

questions.explanation: A converging lens held beyond its focal length forms a real, inverted and diminished image of whatever lies in front of it, on a screen at the far side. The room has to be dark because that image is faint compared with daylight, and the artist works by tracing the projected lines while the light holds, coping with the reversal as the historical recipes advise. Nothing is captured: the result is a drawing, and the projection is only a guide, so composition, proportion and finish remain the artist's. The device cannot improve on a careless eye, and it cannot work without light.
questions.hint: Ask where the image of the bright outdoor scene actually forms, and whether anything is fixed there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a transferred grid does for a design
questions.stem: Before painting, an artist rules a grid of equal squares on the panel, transfers a design onto it, and works out the whole composition inside that grid, measuring the design in a fixed number of units across. What is the grid for?

options.text: It transfers a design proportionately and reduces a complex composition to a repeatable system
It confines the picture to a square, since no part of a design may be worked outside the rule
options.misconception: believes the grid is a boundary rather than a measuring system

options.text: It fills the borders of the panel once the picture is finished, as a decorative last stage
options.misconception: mistakes a working tool for a finished ornament

options.text: It records the painted design itself, so the underdrawing can be checked against it later
options.misconception: confuses the transferred grid with the drawn underdrawing it supports

questions.explanation: Squaring up solves a problem of scale and repetition. A full-size design is divided into units, the same grid is ruled on the destination, and each unit carries its share of the design, so a complex composition can be reproduced proportionally and can be enlarged or reduced without redrawing it. Because the smallest squares can be subdivided again, the same grid also gives the artist a standard of measurement for the figures. It therefore both transfers and disciplines: invention is confined to what the units will hold.
questions.hint: Ask what problem a large, complicated design poses when it has to be reproduced exactly.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify a pigment by its source and price
questions.stem: A chapel's ceiling carries a deep, saturated blue that appears in the site accounts among the most costly materials purchased. Where did that blue come from, and what was it?

options.text: A stone ground to powder and carried over a long route, priced as it was because nothing matched it
A plant grown locally and boiled down, so the expense lay in the labour of a dye works
options.misconception: believes the blue was a dye, though the pigment is a ground mineral

options.text: A blue earth dug from local clay, so the expense lay in hauling very heavy rock
options.misconception: mixes up a local earth pigment with a stone imported from far away

options.text: Ground azurite lightened with white, so the expense lay in grinding a soft copper mineral
options.misconception: substitutes a cheaper copper blue for the rare imported stone

questions.explanation: The deep blue of lapis ultramarine comes from a stone mined in a single known region, in what is now Afghanistan, which was worked for centuries and traded over long distances. The rock is ground, and the valuable blue is separated from the paler waste by washing and settling, so the material cost falls on the best fraction of a large amount of rock. Cheaper blues, including azurite and smalt, were used and substituted for it, and substitution is exactly what the price difference pushed painters towards.
questions.hint: Ask which blue of the period came from a stone dug in one region and carried everywhere else.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what happens when white is mixed into a colour
questions.stem: A painter's dark blue reads almost black, so she grinds a little white lead pigment into it. What does grinding the two pigments together actually do to the colour?

options.text: The white scatters light through the mixture, so the colour rises in value and falls in saturation
The white sinks through the blue, so the mixture darkens and the paint grows heavier
options.misconception: believes particles settle downwards through a mixture instead of mixing into it

options.text: The white replaces the blue particles, so a different pigment altogether is now on the palette
options.misconception: treats mixture as replacement rather than as a combination of both pigments

options.text: The white bleaches the blue chemically, so the pigment loses its colour for ever
options.misconception: invents a chemical bleaching action that has no basis in pigment mixing

questions.explanation: Lead white is made by converting metallic lead into a carbonate, and its particles are very white because they reflect a large share of the light that falls on them, which is what painters mean when they say a white has high tinting power. Ground into a colour, those particles add reflected light to the mixture, so the result is a tint of that colour: lighter, and less saturated because the light is no longer coming from the coloured particles alone. Nothing is destroyed in the mixture and no new pigment is created, which is the difference between mixing and bleaching.
questions.hint: Ask what a white pigment physically is, and what happens to colour when it is present in a mixture.

questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: analyse cropping as a decision about the subject
questions.stem: In a photograph a crowd is caught in motion and two figures are cut in half by the border of the picture, while others stand whole inside it. What has the framing done?

options.text: It has chosen both a moment and a boundary, deciding what counts as part of the event and what does not
It has recorded the whole event, since everything the lens could see was necessarily inside the frame
options.misconception: assumes the frame is the limit of what the camera received

options.text: It has frozen the crowd completely, since a longer exposure would have kept every figure whole
options.misconception: attributes a change of motion to a change of framing

options.text: It has tidied the scene, since cutting a figure at the border arranges the crowd more neatly
options.misconception: treats cropping as tidying up rather than as selection

questions.explanation: A frame is a decision twice over: it fixes an interval of time, and it fixes a portion of a field of view that is larger than the frame itself. What survives the crop, and what is cut in half, is therefore an assertion about what mattered and what was peripheral, not a neutral record. A figure sliced by the border says that the scene continues outside the picture, and successive frames taken from the same position make different selections from the same crowd. Nothing about the choice is a correction of the scene.
questions.hint: Ask how much wider the camera's view is than the frame printed on the paper.

questions.learningObjective: read a pattern of cracks as evidence of a moving support
questions.stem: A conservator's report on a wooden panel records that every crack runs along the grain, that no crack runs across it, and that the work consists of one board. What does that pattern tell the conservator?

options.text: The support has moved, splitting the brittle ground in the direction in which wood moves most
The paint was laid on too thickly and dried badly, cracking within weeks of completion
options.misconception: blames a fault in the paint when the pattern follows the wood

options.text: The panel was struck by something heavy, and the cracks follow the path of the impact
options.misconception: explains a grain-following pattern with a random impact

options.text: The joins were drawn in by a restorer, so the lines were always in the finished picture
options.misconception: treats a physical crack pattern as a documentary addition

questions.explanation: Wood changes most across the grain and least along it, so a ground and paint film sitting on it fail along the grain first and open at the joints between boards. A crack pattern that consistently avoids the grain is therefore a report of movement in the support, not a fault in the paint or the result of an impact, which would scatter cracks without regard to the fibre. Pattern is diagnostic in conservation: the same report also records whether the support is original, whether the work has been thinned, and whether earlier restoration has introduced lines of its own.
questions.hint: Ask in which direction wood changes size most, and what a crack that never crosses the grain is doing.

questions.learningObjective: infer the viewer's position from a painted ceiling
questions.stem: A painted ceiling shows a ring of figures seen from below, their backs, soles and upturned faces turned towards a viewer underneath an opening, and the architecture's receding lines meet at a point above the horizon. What does that tell us?

options.text: The viewer is beneath the ceiling looking up, since receding lines meet above the horizon only then
The viewer is above the ceiling looking down, since the figures are drawn from underneath
options.misconception: reads the described viewpoint as a bird's-eye view of the same room

options.text: The scene is a map seen from directly overhead, since every figure is laid out flat as on a plan
options.misconception: treats a three-dimensional view from below as a flat plan

options.text: The figures are meant to be read from a high gallery, since the architecture is drawn beneath them
options.misconception: inverts the implied viewpoint and locates the viewer in the wrong place

The ceiling's convergence point therefore fixes the viewer as standing underneath and looking up, which is also what the foreshortened soles and upturned faces describe independently. Both facts agree, and that agreement is what makes such pictures convincing. The technique, much used for painted ceilings in the fifteenth century, asks the viewer to accept a real body standing where the architecture is.

questions.learningObjective: read the edges of a canvas as evidence of its history
questions.stem: Around a large oil painting the linen continues past the wooden bars as a wide flat border, folded over and held by small tacks, and those tacks are still in place. What does that tell you about the object?

options.text: The canvas was made up by hand, stretched, and left in that state, so the work is in its original condition
The picture was cut down and relined, since only a second lining leaves tacks standing in the borders
options.misconception: assumes tacks can only survive a relining, when they survive the original stretching

options.text: The work was varnished while still wet, so the tacks were pressed into the soft paint surface
options.misconception: moves the tacks from the stretcher into the paint film

Its state is therefore a record: tacks and folds left as made point to an unaltered stretching, while trimmed edges, filled holes, a reversed tacking strip or a fresh strip of tacks all point to re-stretching, re-lining or cutting down. Those are among the simplest observations to make on a painting and they are often the earliest evidence for how an object has been treated.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: apply the duration of an exposure to what a photograph records
questions.stem: A night photograph shows the lit shopfronts recorded sharply while a person crossing the frame appears as a faint, doubled, translucent shape. What explains the difference between the two?

options.text: The light on the buildings was steady for the whole exposure, while the person was moving throughout it
The camera was focused on the person, so the buildings behind it were recorded less sharply
options.misconception: confuses sharpness due to focus with sharpness due to the subject not moving

options.text: The person moved faster than the shutter could stop, and the frame caught only part of the motion
options.misconception: reads a partly recorded figure as a shutter speed that simply failed

options.text: The shopfronts were photographed a second time afterwards, which is why they look sharper
options.misconception: invents an additional exposure that the description does not report

questions.explanation: A photograph is an integral of light over the exposure, so every point of the scene contributes for the whole interval. Anything stationary records cleanly for as long as the light lasts, and anything that moves leaves a trace spread over the path it travelled, so a figure crossing a frame is doubled, thinned, or faint where it covered each point only briefly. This is why long exposures record the static world and erase the moving one, and why the same street in daylight gives sharp people instead. The exposure fixes an interval, not an event.
questions.hint: Ask what a camera actually does during an exposure, and for how long it does it.

questions.stem: A church panel has gone dull and yellow-brown, and after an old layer of varnish is removed the colours underneath look far more saturated than before. What was the varnish doing, and what is the cost of taking it off?

options.text: It saturated and protected the colours, and removing it changes the picture for ever, because that state is lost
It dulled and protected the colours, and removing it simply returns the picture to what the painter left
options.misconception: claims that removal is a perfect restoration of the original surface

options.text: It faded and protected the colours, and removing it is a routine cleaning with no lasting effect
options.misconception: confuses the yellowing of the varnish with fading in the paint beneath it

options.text: It protected the colours without changing them, and removing it returns an exact original surface
options.misconception: denies that varnish alters the appearance of the picture at all

questions.explanation: A varnish is a clear resinous film laid on a dry picture, and it works by filling the surface so that light passes into the paint and comes back out through a continuous medium, which deepens and saturates the colour and protects a fragile film from handling and dirt. Old resin varnases oxidise and turn yellow, so the picture is now seen through a discoloured layer and looks duller than it did. Once that layer is removed, the state it concealed is gone for good, and a conservator has to weigh that against the gain.
questions.hint: Ask what a clear coating does to the light coming back out of a paint layer, and where the yellow now is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: interpret measured perspective evidence
questions.stem: A survey of a constructed interior measures, in centimetres from the left edge of the picture: the orthogonals of the left wall meet at x = 118, y = 96; those of the right wall also meet at x = 118, y = 96; the horizon falls at y = 96; and the eyes of a standing figure in the room are at y = 96. What does the survey establish?

options.text: A single vanishing point on the horizon at eye level, so a standing adult is implied inside the room
Two separate vanishing points, so the room is being constructed in a two-point perspective
options.misconception: counts two walls and mistakes them for two vanishing points

options.text: No vanishing point at all, since lines that agree cannot have been drawn by the artist
options.misconception: reads agreement between two sets of lines as evidence of a later addition

options.text: A single point below the horizon, so the viewer must be looking up towards the ceiling
options.misconception: misreads a measurement on the horizon as a point beneath it

questions.explanation: Two sets of orthogonals that agree on the same point describe one vanishing point, not two, and that is what makes the construction one-point: all the orthogonals in the picture are parallel to one another. The point sits on the horizon because orthogonals run at eye level, and the third measurement places the horizon at the same height as a standing figure's eyes, so the implied viewer is a standing adult at that height. Measurements like these are the physical ground of a claim about viewpoint, and they are what lets a later scholar check whether a set of lines was added.
questions.hint: Ask how many points the two walls share, and what the agreement of the three heights means.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Paint film thickness as a record of technique
questions.learningObjective: interpret measured film thickness
questions.stem: A survey of an oil painting records the thickest point of the paint film in several areas: 0.06 millimetres in the sky, 0.08 in the flesh, 0.24 at the white of a collar, and 0.31 in the highlights of a sleeve. What can a conservator conclude from those figures?

options.text: Paint was laid in thin layers almost everywhere and in a thick body only in the highlights, as an impasto technique intends
The picture was painted thickly throughout, and the thin passages were cleaned back towards the ground
options.misconception: reads uniform impasto with later abrasion as the method used throughout

options.text: The thin passages are the original paint and the thick ones are later overpaint added in restoration
options.misconception: takes heavy passages to be restoration rather than to be a technique

options.text: The figures date the picture, since film thickness follows a fixed recipe in each century
options.misconception: believes film thickness is a dating formula rather than a record of working method

questions.explanation: A film a fraction of a millimetre thick is a normal thin layer, and a film several times thicker is a body of paint standing above the surface. The pattern here, thin everywhere and thick only where light is to be caught, is the signature of paint applied heavily in the highlights and used as material, and it is the pattern a palette knife produces. Measurement therefore records the method rather than the date, and the two have to be read separately: thickness says how the picture was built up, and it is a poor dating signal because painters of any period have used impasto.
questions.hint: Ask what a thickness three or four times the rest of the picture is doing in the paint.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: infer the sequence of work from a cross-section
questions.stem: A cross-section taken through a panel and photographed under magnification shows, from the wood outward: eight coats of chalk and glue; a layer of gold leaf; a dark brushed line; a layer of red earth; a thin blue layer; a clear coating. What does the section establish about the order of work?

options.text: A gilded ground, then a brushed underdrawing, then paint built up in layers, then a protective coating
Paint, then gilding, then underdrawing, so the panel was worked in the reverse of the usual order
options.misconception: reads a conventional bottom-up sequence as though the picture were built from the top down

options.text: A coating, then paint, then gilding, which shows the whole panel was turned upside down to work
options.misconception: infers an upside-down working method from an ordinary preparation layer

options.text: Gilding, then coating, then underdrawing, so the design was transferred after the varnish went on
options.misconception: puts the varnish before the underdrawing, which is a procedure nobody uses

questions.explanation: A cross-section is a stratigraphy, and layers are read from the support outwards in the order they were applied. Chalk and glue is the ground, because it is always on the wood; gold leaf over the ground is the gilded field; the dark brushed line lies on top of the gold, so it is a drawing made after gilding; the red earth and the blue are the paint, built up on that; and the clear coating last, because a varnish goes on a dry picture. Every stage constrains the next, since each needs a dry, firm surface to sit on.
questions.hint: Ask which layer must be applied to the bare wood, and which must be laid over dry paint.

questions.topic: A widening join in a panel
questions.learningObjective: interpret a measured gap as movement of the support
questions.stem: A conservator's measurements on a two-board panel record a gap along the join between the boards of 0.2 millimetres at the top edge and 2.3 millimetres at the bottom edge, with the grain of both boards running along their length. What does that pattern show?

options.text: The join has opened most at the bottom, so the panel has moved with the seasons and the ground has failed along it
The join has closed at the bottom, so the panel has contracted downwards and pulled itself together
options.misconception: reads a widening gap as a closing one and reverses the sign of the movement

options.text: The join was badly glued from the start, so the gap has been present since the panel was made
options.misconception: blames the original construction for a movement the pattern records as later

options.text: The figures date the panel, since the width of a join is fixed by workshop convention
options.misconception: believes a measured gap is a dating formula rather than a record of movement

questions.explanation: A gap that is four times wider at the bottom than at the top has opened downwards, which is the ordinary behaviour of a wide panel as its boards move across the grain and try to cup. The opening is largest where the bending is greatest, and the ground above the join fails along the line of weakness, which is where a crack will be found. Nothing in the pattern points to the glue or the carpenter: a fixed gap would be the same width all the way up, and the seasonal difference in width is itself the evidence that the support is still responding to the room it is in.
questions.hint: Ask whether a gap that is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom is opening or closing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A pigment account and the choice of blue
questions.learningObjective: interpret a purchase record as evidence of substitution
questions.stem: A church's account book records, for one season, twelve ounces of lead white, two ounces of the imported blue stone and forty ounces of the local copper blue, at prices of one, twelve and two florins the ounce. What does that purchase suggest about the finished ceiling?

options.text: The imported blue was used sparingly, and most of the ceiling was painted in the cheaper local substitute
The ceiling was painted entirely in the imported blue, and the other two pigments were for the frame
options.misconception: ignores a purchase far too small to have covered the whole ceiling

options.text: The two blues were mixed together everywhere, giving the ceiling a single intermediate colour
options.misconception: assumes every pigment bought was mixed with every other pigment bought

options.text: The local blue was bought by mistake, since copper blue cannot be used in a wall painting
options.misconception: supposes the cheaper pigment was unusable in the technique described

questions.explanation: The quantities and the prices describe a working economy. Forty ounces of the cheap blue at two florins is far more material than two ounces of the stone at twelve, so the great majority of the surface must have been painted in the substitute, and the expensive pigment has to have been reserved for a small part of the scheme, typically the most important figure or the most prominent garment. Accounts of this kind are among the best evidence for how a picture was actually made, because they record purchases rather than intentions, and they explain why so many large surfaces look consistent in colour.
questions.hint: Ask how much surface the largest quantity could cover, and where the expensive pigment could have been reserved.

questions.topic: Measuring a picture in subdivided units
questions.learningObjective: apply a measured grid to count design units
questions.stem: A conservator's drawing of a panel records a horizon near the top of the picture and a distance of 75 centimetres from that line down to the bottom edge, a span ruled into thirty equal divisions. If every one of those divisions is then halved, how many small squares run from the horizon to the bottom edge?

options.text: Sixty, because halving every division doubles the number of equal units across the same span
Thirty, because halving the divisions does not change the number of units in the span
options.misconception: believes the count stays the same after the units are made smaller

options.text: Fifteen, because halving the divisions halves the number of units in the span
options.misconception: divides the count instead of multiplying it when the unit is halved

options.text: Ninety, because halving each division adds an extra unit to every original division
options.misconception: assumes three units appear for every two that were there before

questions.explanation: A grid of thirty divisions spans a fixed measured distance, so the number of equal units across that distance depends only on how small the unit is made. Halving each division replaces every whole unit with two half-units, so the count doubles, to sixty, and each of the sixty measures 75 divided by 60, which is 1.25 centimetres. Subdividing in this way is standard practice, because the smaller unit is then used as a fixed measure for the figures, which is what makes a large composition repeatable rather than improvised.
questions.hint: Ask how many half-units fit into one whole unit, and then multiply.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Working time and the absence of blending
questions.learningObjective: use a binder's drying behaviour to infer a working method
questions.stem: A survey of a panel reports that no passage contains a blended transition between two colours, and that the surface is built from many small strokes laid in one direction, with a monochrome layer underneath. First state what the binder does to working time, and then say what the report implies.

options.text: The binder sets in minutes, so the picture was built from small hatched strokes with no blending wet at all
The binder sets by slow oxidation, so the absence of blending means the work was done on a dry wall
options.misconception: gives tempera the oil binder's behaviour and borrows a wall technique

options.text: The binder never dries at all, so the absence of blending means a printed design was copied
options.misconception: supplies a non-drying binder and an implausible working method

options.text: The binder cures to a hard film, so the absence of blending means paint was scraped back after drying
options.misconception: invents a scraping stage that the report describes as clean passage

questions.explanation: The report is describing egg tempera, and both of its features follow from one fact: the binder sets in minutes as the water leaves, so there is no open time in which one colour can be worked into another. Form is therefore built from many small strokes laid side by side over a monochrome underpainting, which is why the strokes run in a consistent direction and why the light passes through thin layers. The alternative explanation, an oil on a dry wall, is ruled out by the surface itself, since oil on plaster has no ground and no underpainting.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two things in the report could only be explained by a binder that closes quickly.
