questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the plaster does, and what cannot be undone
questions.learningObjective: derive a conservation limit from a fresco's construction
questions.stem: A wall painting has a small area where the paint and a layer of plaster below it have both flaked away, and the surrounding surface is sound. First say what the plaster does to a pigment applied to it, and then say what that allows a conservator to do.

options.text: It locks the colour into itself as it hardens, so a loss cannot be cleaned off or replaced without taking wall with it
It stays chemically inert, so the loss can simply be repainted in the same pigment and tone
options.misconception: assumes an inert wall allows loss to be filled without touching the wall itself

options.text: It dissolves in water, so the loss can be washed back and repainted while the patch is still damp
options.misconception: gives lime plaster a solubility in water that it does not have once set

options.text: It hardens under the varnish, so the loss can be restored by adding a fresh protective coating
options.misconception: makes a new varnish restore pigment that is no longer on the wall

questions.explanation: In a fresco the pigment is inside the plaster, carried by the water of the wet coat and locked in as the lime carbonates, so the picture is not a layer on the wall but a part of its fabric. A flaked loss has therefore taken both colour and wall with it, and nothing can be cleaned off or painted into the gap without removing more plaster. Conservators work by consolidating the surviving plaster and stopping the loss, not by repainting the missing patch, and any decision to fill a loss is a decision about how much of the original to replace.
questions.hint: Ask whether the colour in a buon fresco is a layer or a part of the wall material.

questions.topic: Locating the vanishing point and the viewer
questions.learningObjective: infer the implied viewer from a perspective construction
questions.stem: In a constructed interior the orthogonals of the floor and the two side walls all meet at one point, and that point lies level with the eyes of a standing figure in the room. First say where the point lies, and then say what the second fact tells you.

options.text: It lies on the horizon, and since the horizon is at eye level a standing adult is implied inside the room
It lies above the horizon, and that means the viewer is standing in the room looking down
options.misconception: puts the point above the horizon and reads it as a downward view

options.text: It lies at the centre of the picture, so the viewer is standing at the room's exact middle
options.misconception: confuses the point of convergence with the centre of the support

options.text: It lies on the ground line, so the viewer is crouching down at the level of the pavement
options.misconception: reads the point as a point on the base of the scene rather than on the horizon

questions.explanation: Orthogonals of a single plane parallel to the picture plane all meet at one point on the horizon line, because every one of them runs at the level of the eye. So the first step fixes the point's position, and the second observation supplies the height: since the point is level with the eyes of a standing figure, the implied viewer is a standing adult of that height at that position in the room. Together the two facts say that the picture was built for a body to occupy that space, which is why such interiors are hung at the eye level of a visitor.
questions.hint: Ask which line all orthogonals of one plane must share, and what height that line records.

questions.topic: Relief, light, and the limits of a photograph
questions.learningObjective: apply a raised paint surface to the question of reproduction
questions.stem: A passage of an oil painting has been built up in thick body, so that ridges of paint and the scrape of a knife stand above the surface. First say what that relief does to the way the passage is lit, and then say what it means for reproducing the picture.

options.text: The ridges catch light and throw small shadows, so a photograph fixes one lighting that a moving viewer never sees
The ridges reflect light evenly, so a photograph reproduces exactly what a moving viewer sees
options.misconception: claims an even reflection that would make the painting invisible as material

options.text: The ridges absorb the light, so the passage is always darker than the rest of the picture
options.misconception: makes relief darken a passage, when it redistributes the light over it

options.text: The ridges scatter light equally in every direction, so the passage looks the same from any angle
options.misconception: believes a raised surface cannot depend on where the light is coming from

questions.explanation: A raised passage is not a drawn shape but a piece of material, so it is lit differently from different positions: the ridge takes the light and the hollow beside it throws a small shadow, and as the viewer moves those highlights travel. A photograph collapses all of that into a single lighting condition fixed by the position of the camera and the lamps, so the picture in the record is one moment of a mobile effect. The consequence is that a reproduction is evidence about the paint and the composition, never about the viewer's experience of the surface.
questions.hint: Ask what a photograph does with a surface that changes appearance as the viewer moves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of work on a fresco wall
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of painting a fresco wall
questions.stem: A wall painting in buon fresco has to be executed in a fixed order, because each stage needs a surface with a particular state. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: The fine plaster is laid fresh over one section and painted while it is still wet
A coarse rough plaster is spread over the wall and left to harden before anything else
The design is transferred to that rough plaster and the whole area is scored into sections
Finishing details and corrections are added later onto the surface after it has dried

questions.explanation: The order is forced by the state of the surface at each step. A rough coat goes on first and must dry, because a design cannot be drawn on wet plaster and a later coat will not bond to a wet one. The design is transferred to that dry rough coat, since the fine plaster will be opaque and would hide it. The fine plaster is then laid in sections and painted while damp, because that is the only moment colour will enter the wall. Anything applied to the dry surface afterwards is a different technique altogether, bound to the wall rather than fused with it.
questions.hint: Ask which surface each stage needs, and whether it has to be dry or still damp for the next one.

questions.topic: The order of work on a gilded panel
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of painting a gilded panel
questions.stem: A panel that will be gilded and then painted in egg tempera is worked in a set order, and each step depends on the one before being completely dry. Put these five stages into that order.

options.text: A monochrome underpainting fixes the light and shade, and the finished colour is built over it
A protective coating is laid over the dry picture at the very end of the work
The board is sized, covered in coats of chalk and glue, and polished to a smooth white ground
A full-size design is transferred to that ground, and its lines are drawn onto the surface
The gilded field is laid over the dry ground and burnished into a continuous surface

questions.explanation: Ground first, because gold leaf needs a firm, even, absorbent surface to bond to, and a burnished leaf needs the ground to be completely dry. The design comes after the gold, because the drawing is made on the finished gilded field and its lines are the ones that guide the paint. The underpainting follows the drawing, and only when that is dry can the colour be built over it, since tempera will not merge with a damp layer. The protective coating is last, and only after the picture is dry, because it is meant to seal the surface rather than become part of the painting.
questions.hint: Ask which step needs bare wood, and which step has to come before anything is laid over the gold.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that produce a photographic print
questions.stem: A photograph has to travel from the moment of exposure to a finished print, and at each stage the image has to be made permanent before the next one begins. Put these five stages into the order in which they occur.

options.text: The negative is developed and fixed, so that the latent image it holds becomes permanent
The finished print is washed, dried, and then mounted or framed for viewing
A sheet of sensitised paper is exposed against the negative as a small proof print
The chosen negative is enlarged onto a larger sheet, which is then developed and fixed
The scene is exposed on film, and the film is taken into the darkroom to be developed

questions.explanation: Exposure records a latent image, which is not yet stable and has to be developed and fixed before it will survive being handled, so the negative comes first. Only a fixed negative can be laid against a sheet of sensitised paper, and the small proof print made from it is how an image is judged and chosen, since enlarging every frame would be wasteful. The chosen frame is then enlarged and developed and fixed in turn, because the enlarged image is equally latent at first. Washing and drying come last, since a print that is still wet cannot be handled, mounted or framed.
questions.hint: Ask what the exposure produces, and what has to be fixed before it can be used to make anything else.

questions.topic: Working out what an unknown panel is

The support, its construction, its condition and any old labels are examined and recorded

The support and its condition are recorded first, because the material, the construction and any old labels set the frame of everything else, and because handling decisions made in the first hour can destroy evidence. Analysis then identifies what the panel is actually made of, which fixes the range of dates and places it could come from. Only then can the painted handling and the underdrawing be read as evidence, and only then is a comparison with dated works worth making. The conclusion comes last and has to carry its own uncertainty.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be known about the object itself before anything can be compared with anything else.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the binder sets the working time
questions.learningObjective: explain how a binder's drying behaviour shapes a method
questions.stem: A painter can spend an afternoon working a passage in oil, but the same passage in egg tempera would have to be abandoned within minutes. Explain why the binder changes the working time so much, and what follows from that for the surfaces the two media can produce.

answer.exemplar: Egg tempera dries by losing water to the air, and it does so quickly: a passage is workable for minutes rather than hours. That single fact reorganises the method, because there is no window in which one colour can be worked into another, so a wet stroke laid beside a dry one leaves a visible edge and a new stroke over a dry one lifts the earlier film instead of merging with it. Form is therefore built from many small strokes laid side by side, usually over a monochrome underpainting that has already decided the light and shade, and depth is created by hatching and by the white ground and the underpainment showing through thin layers. Oil behaves differently because it does not lose a solvent; the oil itself is the binder, and it hardens by slow reaction with oxygen from the air. Linseed oil, with its high content of unsaturated fatty acids, is drying precisely because of that unsaturation. Hours or days of working time follow from it, and that time buys blending, wet-into-wet work, thick impasto, and the layering of translucent glazes one over another. The two media therefore do not merely dry at different speeds: they make different pictures, one built from small marks and light coming through layers, the other from blended transitions and modelled, sometimes three-dimensional, paint. The costs go with the benefits, since an oil surface skins over while it sets, traps dust, and cannot be varnished for months.

questions.explanation: A full answer names the mechanism, not just the speed: saying that one medium dries quickly and the other slowly restates the question. What earns credit is the two different physical processes, the working time each one gives, the techniques that follow from having or lacking that time, and the surfaces those techniques produce. A weak response describes only the tempera side, or gives the chemistry without drawing the consequence for the picture.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen to the binder in each case, and how long it takes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain the construction of a fresco and its consequences for loss
questions.stem: A wall painter is given a fresh coat of lime plaster and a morning to use it. Explain what the plaster does to the colour applied to it, and what that means for a conservator who later finds a patch where both paint and plaster have flaked away.

answer.exemplar: Lime plaster dries by taking up carbon dioxide from the air, and as it becomes carbonate it grows a crystalline network that locks in whatever is suspended in it. A pigment brushed into the water of a freshly laid coat is therefore carried into the wall itself rather than sitting on it, which is why the surface of a fresco is matte, why the picture cannot be cleaned with solvent without removing plaster as well, and why a detached section of a fresco is a piece of wall rather than a skin. The method accepts one great restriction to gain one great advantage: a patch must be finished while the plaster is still workable, so the wall is worked in day-sized sections and the composition is planned around the joins. For the conservator the consequence is severe. Where paint and plaster have flaked away, there is no original layer left to clean back, clean off, or repaint into, and no solvent can be used on the surrounding surface without risk to it. Treatment therefore means consolidating what remains and arresting the loss, and any decision to fill the gap with new material is a decision about how much of the original to replace, which is a judgement about interpretation as much as about technique.

questions.explanation: A full answer treats the plaster as the cause and not merely as the background: it has to say that the colour becomes part of the wall, and then follow that through to what a conservator can and cannot do. What earns credit is the distinction between treating a loss and replacing one, since the missing material is wall as well as colour. A weak response says only that fresco is permanent, or only that the technique is fast, and never reaches the conservation question the stem asks about.
questions.hint: Ask whether the colour is a layer on the wall or part of the wall, and what follows from the answer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a photograph fixes and leaves out
questions.learningObjective: explain the temporal and spatial limits of a photographic record
questions.stem: A photograph of a public demonstration shows a banner at one edge cut in half by the frame and a speaker in the middle of the field. Explain what a photograph fixes and what it excludes, and say why the cut banner is a decision rather than an accident of the medium.

answer.exemplar: A photograph is an integral of light over a finite interval, and that is the source of both its power and its limits. Everything that reflects light onto the film during the exposure contributes, so stationary things record cleanly and anything that moves leaves a trace of the path it travelled; a figure crossing the frame can be doubled, thinned, or nearly lost. Nothing before the exposure or after it is recorded at all, so the image is a consequence of when the shutter was opened, and of the aim of the person who opened it. Spatially the limit is the frame, which selects a portion of a field of view that is always larger than the print; the camera can see more than the picture keeps. A banner sliced by the border is therefore a decision with two parts. It says the demonstration continued outside the picture, and it concentrates attention on what was kept. Framing of that kind is a normal part of making the picture, and it is one reason a photograph is evidence about a photographer's judgement as much as about an event. The temptation is to treat the frame as a neutral window, or as a fault to be corrected by including the whole scene; both mistakes remove the only part of the record that is the photographer's.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to make two separate limits, one of time and one of field, and then show that the cut banner is a choice made inside the second of them. What earns credit is the statement that an exposure integrates light over an interval, so motion smears and the moment is chosen. A weak response says only that a photograph is a snapshot, which leaves the field of view unexplained, or treats the crop as a fault that a wider lens would have fixed.
questions.hint: Ask what happens during an exposure, and how much wider the view is than the frame.

questions.topic: Why a gold ground leaves space undetermined
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of a gold ground on depicted space
questions.stem: A gilded panel shows a standing saint, a kneeling donor and a small piece of architecture, all set against a field of gold leaf with no floor, no sky and no horizon. Explain why that field does so little for the space of the picture, and say how it changes the way the figures are read.

answer.exemplar: Gold leaf is achromatic and non-representational. It names no place, no hour and no light source, and it supplies none of the cues by which a viewer locates a figure: there is no ground line to stand on, no horizon, no scale, no recession and no cast shadow. A figure set against it is therefore not somewhere at all, and that is the effect wanted in a church, where the subject is a saint rather than a place. It also changes the status of the figures. Freed from a setting, the saint is presented directly to the viewer and read as a presence, while the small kneeling donor is read not as a person standing in a room but as a prayer offered in front of something larger. The few hints of architecture that do appear are read the same way, as an attribute rather than as a setting, because the gold has already ruled out the alternative. Painters who wanted real space did not remove the gold; they kept it for the figures and the frame and introduced sky and landscape behind, which is what produces the uneasy mixture of two incompatible kinds of space running through so many altarpieces.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to say what the gold cannot do, since a description of gold as bright or shimmering explains nothing about space. What earns credit is the list of absent cues, the absence of a place, and the consequence that the figures are read as a presence addressed to the viewer rather than as people in a room. A weak response explains the gold's beauty or its cost, neither of which bears on the question of how the figures are read.
questions.hint: Ask what a metal surface can tell a viewer about place, distance and light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Number of vanishing points for an oblique set of edges
questions.learningObjective: count the vanishing points for a set of receding parallel edges
questions.stem: In a perspective construction, a set of parallel edges that recede at an angle to the picture plane, and is not parallel to it, converges on how many vanishing points?
questions.explanation: A set of parallel edges can only be parallel to the picture plane, or oblique to it, and the two cases behave differently. Edges parallel to the picture plane stay parallel in the picture, so they contribute no vanishing point at all, which is why the far wall of a room is drawn as a rectangle. Edges oblique to it converge, and they converge on a point on the horizon. One-point perspective, the case taught first, is simply the special arrangement in which the two horizontal directions of the room are one parallel to the picture plane and one perpendicular to it, so only one set converges. Turn the same box a little and the second direction becomes oblique as well, a second point appears on the horizon, and the construction becomes two-point. A third point appears only for a third direction of edges that is neither parallel nor perpendicular.
questions.hint: Ask how many directions that set of parallel edges has once perspective is applied to it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: compute a ratio of depicted heights as evidence of rank
questions.stem: A carved relief shows a standing ruler whose carved height is 1.5 metres, standing on the same ground line as two captives whose carved height is 0.5 metres. How many times taller than a captive is the ruler in this carving?
questions.explanation: Dividing 1.5 by 0.5 gives three, so the ruler is carved at three times the height of the captives beside him. The measurement is the useful part, because it removes the vague talk about importance and states a relationship that any reader of the relief can check. The threefold difference is a claim about rank, not about distance: the figures share one ground line and one setting, so nothing in the carving invites an optical reading, and the eye takes the difference in size as a statement of order. A useful caution is that the same ratio would mean something quite different in a picture that established depth convincingly, where relative size is the ordinary measure of how far away things stand. The two rules can also be used deliberately against each other, as they are whenever an artist wants a figure to seem both important and far away.
questions.hint: Ask how many captive heights fit into the height of the ruler.
